summary: Updates the IPPM Framework from RFC 2330 with expanded stream parameters and measurement considerations, because modern networks are not always steadily connected.

plainLanguage.summary: Network measurement used to assume a path that behaves predictably and never learns. RFC 7312 explains why that assumption no longer holds, and gives the extra care that measurement methods need now: how to choose packet sizes and contents, what to record about what was sent, and how to judge whether a method is repeatable.

questions: advanced sampling framework for network measurement
why is continuity deprecated in ippm
subtitle: What to watch out for when measuring a modern network, where the network reacts to your own test traffic.

tldr.problem: The measurement framework used for years assumes a path that behaves the same way every time and keeps no memory of what it has already sent. Modern networks break both assumptions, so two measurements of the same path can disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with the path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates the framework with a definition of reactive path behaviour, a set of extra stream and packet parameters to control and record, and a revised set of criteria for judging whether a measurement method is any good.
tldr.outcome: The metric definitions themselves are left alone. What changes is the advice on how to measure with them, including a new rule that a method cannot always be conservative about the network it measures.

facts.label: Delay effect on HSPA
facts.value: More than 200% increase from small rate changes

facts.value: Deprecated as an alternative to repeatability

today: RFC 7312 is an Informational RFC published in August 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2330 with measurement-methodology guidance while leaving the existing metric definitions valid.

sections.title: The Assumption That Broke
sections.content:
The IPPM working group created a framework for metric development that has stood the test of time and enabled many fundamental metrics, updated only once in a specific area. That framework generally relies on several assumptions, one of which is not explicitly stated but assumed: lightly loaded paths conform to the linear equation that serialization delay equals packet size divided by capacity, and they are stateless or history-less, with some exceptions such as firewalls.

That does not hold true for many modern network technologies. Reactive paths, those with demand-driven resource allocation, and links with time-slotted operation both behave differently. Per-flow state can be observed on test packet streams, and if that is not taken into account it will influence the characterisation of the network. Flow history also affects the performance of applications and is perceived by their users.

The framework explicitly recommends repeatable measurement metrics and methodologies, and measurements in today's access networks show that its methodological guidelines have to be extended to capture the reactive nature of these networks. Some link types show distinct responses to repeated measurements with identical stimulus, that is, identical traffic patterns, and fine-tuning the measurement traffic patterns can improve continuity and repeatability for those link types.

The central new idea is reactive path behaviour: a repeatable phenomenon where packet transfer performance characteristics change according to prior observations of the packet flow of interest, at the reactive host or link. It is nominally deterministic with respect to the flow of interest. A sender may not have absolute control of the ingress packet stream characteristics at a reactive host or link, but that does not change the deterministic reactions present there. Examples include links with active and inactive state detectors, and hosts or links that revise their traffic serving and forwarding rates up or down based on packet arrival history. Apart from the size of the payload at the layer of interest and the header itself, packet content does not influence the measurement, so any indication of reactive behaviour has to name the layer at which the measurement was made.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network equipment notices what you are sending it and changes its behaviour because of it. Measure the same path twice and you get two different answers, not because the path changed but because the equipment remembered the first time.

sections.title: What to Control and What to Record
sections.content:
Four areas need attention. The first is the definition of the test packet. Network treatment depends on the fullest extent on the packet of Type-P definition, and state is often kept on a per-flow basis at various points in the path, so significant treatment differences occur with the simplest of Type-P parameters, the packet length; using several lengths is recommended. Payload optimisation in intermediate segments, such as compression or format conversion, breaks the convention of payload correspondence when measurements are made at different points along a path. Two further Type-P parameters are recommended: packet length and payload type.

On packet length, many instances of network characterisation have relied on a single test packet length, while benchmarking methods have used a range of fixed lengths and frequently augmented fixed-size tests with a mixture of sizes, or Internet Mix, as described in the IMIX Genome document. Packet length influences delay measurements, because the one-way delay metric includes serialization time in its first-bit to last-bit timestamping requirements. Different sizes can have a much larger influence on link delay and delay variation than serialization alone would explain, and the effect can be non-linear. To eliminate packet length as a source of uncertainty, successive measurements must use identical traffic patterns; in practice a combination of random payload and random start time can yield representative results.

On payload content, the drive for efficient network resource use has put compression on some links, and the optimiser may drop parts of a file that it considers unimportant, which includes measurement packets when they use plain-text payloads. Measurements should add payload content as a Type-P parameter, and optimisers can be ruled out by using incompressible payload, supplied by a pseudo-random sequence generator or by using part of a compressed file. Optimisation can also go beyond one stream, with header compression and voice aggregation, and the more concurrent flows an intermediate host treats, the higher the incentive to aggregate them, which can make the flows influence each other's timing far beyond the usual queueing effect.

The second area is packet history. The recent history and the instantaneous data rate influence measurement results for reactive links, and small changes in history, such as packets lost along the path, can cause large performance variations. Delay in reactive third-generation networks such as HSPA depends to a large extent on the test traffic data rate, and small changes in that rate can be the reason of more than a 200 per cent increase in delay, depending on the packet size. The third area is that the access technology may change during testing, and today several access technologies can present the same physical interface to the host, which makes it hard to tell an access change apart from reactive behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: To get the same answer twice, you have to send the same thing twice: the same sizes, in a form the network cannot quietly compress, and you have to record what you sent so that anyone reading the results can see it.

sections.title: Time-Slotted Networks Cancel Randomness
sections.content:
Time-slotted operation of interfaces, routers or links along a path is a particular challenge, especially when the time-slot period is substantial. The central observation, as an extension to Poisson stream sampling, is that the first such time-slotted component cancels unbiased measurement stream sampling. In the worst case, time-slotted operation converts an unbiased random measurement packet stream into a periodic packet stream, and those heavily biased packets may then interact with the periodic behaviour of later time-slotted elements.

Sources of this effect can be found in virtually any system, network component or path, with system clock resolution and operating system ticks among the examples, and their impact on measurements is a matter of the order of magnitude compared with the metric under observation. The amount of bias depends on the measurement stream, the relative offset between allocated time slots in later path elements, the delay variation in the path and other sources of variation. Results might change over time, depending on how accurately the sending host, the receiving host and the time-slotted components are synchronised to each other and to global time. Where path segments keep flow state, a change of flow parameters or a reallocation can cause substantial variation.

Practical measurements confirm that this interference limits the delay measurement variation to a subset of the theoretical value range, and that the samples can aggregate on artificial limits, producing distributions with more than one mode. The choice of measurement methodology for a time-slotted path depends largely on the viewpoint. End-to-end metrics give accurate results for short-term sessions and where flow state is unlikely to be modified, and an application trying to approximate path performance over a few minutes under stable conditions should prefer them. If the goal is a long-term forecast of time-slotted path performance, a segmented approach relying on subpath metrics is preferred, because regenerating unbiased measurement traffic at each hop reveals the true range of performance for all the segments.
sections.plainLanguage: Some equipment only gets a turn at fixed moments, like a door that opens on the hour. A test stream that arrives at random times is turned into a regular one by the first such door, and everything measured afterwards is distorted.

sections.title: How to Judge a Measurement Method
sections.content:
Repeatability is the central criterion. The original framework says a methodology should be repeatable: if it is used multiple times under identical conditions, the same measurements should result. The RFC develops this into an objective, measurable criterion. The criteria of equivalent results agreed in the IPPM advancement process serve as the surrogate for interoperability when assessing metric RFCs, expressed as objective statistical requirements for comparison across the same implementations and independent implementations in the test plans specific to each RFC. The revised wording is that the methods should produce equivalent measurement results.

Continuity is retired as an alternative criterion. It said a methodology exhibits continuity if, for small variations in conditions, it results in small variations in the resulting measurements. There are conditions where metrics may exhibit continuity, and others where the criterion would fail for both user traffic and active measurement traffic. Link fragmentation is one example: the delay rises non-linearly when the packet size goes just beyond the limit of a single fragment, and an active measurement packet sees the same increase. Most TCP implementations also exhibit non-linear performance over some part of their operating region, so that an incremental improvement to a path can result in lower overall throughput. The time-slotted elements described earlier qualify as a further exception. Continuity is therefore deprecated in favour of the more exact evaluation of repeatability.

Usefulness is extended to actionable. The original framework says metrics must be useful to users and providers in understanding the performance they experience or provide. The extension says that metrics must enable users and operators to understand path performance and should help to direct corrective actions when warranted, based on the measurement results. Anomaly detection is an important first step, but central to maintenance is isolating the root cause down to a specific subpath, link or host, and metrics should support that second step too, which consists of specific, directed on-demand measurements.

Conservativeness is qualified. The original idea is that the act of measurement does not modify, or only slightly modifies, the value of the metric being measured. That depends on the technology of the measurement path, and when deployed on reactive paths the measurement packets can themselves cause capacity to be allocated or reallocated. Small measurement flow variations can also make other users on the same path see significant variations. It is therefore not always possible for the method to be conservative.

Two further points close the section. Spatial composition, which estimates the performance of a whole path from subpath metrics, supports unbiased sampling, and where a time-slotted link makes unbiased measurement of every segment infeasible, restoring randomness of the samples where needed is recommended in combination with it. And where a path element with reactive behaviour is sensitive to flow inactivity, it is recommended to truncate the tail of the Poisson distribution so that the random gap between packets is never long enough to change the element's state; tail truncation has been used without issue to keep minimum sample sizes attainable within a fixed test interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC tightens one test of a measurement method and drops another. Two runs should now give equivalent results, which is a harder test than "small changes, small differences". It also admits that measuring a network can change the network.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Safeguarding repeatability as a key property of measurement methodologies is highly challenging and sometimes impossible in reactive paths. Measurements in paths with demand-driven allocation strategies must use a prototypical application packet stream in order to infer a specific application's performance. Measurement repetition with unbiased network and flow states, for example by rebooting the measurement hosts, can help to avoid interference with periodic network behaviour, with randomness being a mandatory feature for avoiding correlation with network timing.

Inferring the path performance between one measurement session or packet stream and other sessions or streams with different characteristics is generally discouraged with reactive paths, because of the huge set of global parameters that influence instantaneous path performance.
sections.plainLanguage: There are networks where you simply cannot get the same answer twice. When that is true, the honest thing is to measure the way the real application would behave, rather than to pretend the path is more predictable than it is.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live paths are relevant here as well, and the RFC points to the one-way and two-way active measurement protocol documents for them.

On privacy, the sensitive information available to potential observers is greatly reduced when using active techniques within the scope of this work, since the test packets are dedicated to measurement and do not monitor user traffic. Passive observation of user traffic for measurement purposes raises many privacy issues, and the RFC refers the reader to the privacy considerations described in the large scale measurement of broadband performance framework, which covers both active and passive techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring with your own test packets keeps you away from other people's traffic, which is the privacy advantage of active measurement.

viz.caption: THE OLD ASSUMPTION AND THE COMMON CASE TODAY

left.title: Assumed by the original framework
left.desc: A lightly loaded path with no memory: delay follows packet size divided by capacity, and the same traffic gives the same answer every time.

right.title: Common today
right.desc: A reactive path that remembers what it has recently seen and changes its behaviour because of it, so the same traffic gives a different answer.

viz.caption: FOUR THINGS A MEASUREMENT METHOD MUST NOW HANDLE

items.title: The test packet itself
items.text: Choose the length and the payload content, and record them, so the network cannot treat two runs differently.

items.title: Packet history
items.text: Recent traffic at the device under test changes the results, so it has to be known.

items.title: Access technology change
items.text: The host may move to a different access method mid-test, which has to be told apart from reactive behaviour.

items.title: Time-slotted links
items.text: A link that only passes traffic at fixed times turns a random stream into a regular one.

viz.caption: THE CRITERIA FOR A GOOD MEASUREMENT METHOD

cells: The methods should produce equivalent measurement results
A relaxed alternative test of repeatability
Metrics must help users understand performance
Extended to actionable: results should point to a corrective action
Measurement should barely change what is measured
It is not always possible on a reactive path
